shadow.$description: The four axes a box-shadow is made of, as raw material. There is deliberately NO composite step here. Clustering the axes into a usable box-shadow is the semantic act — it says which combination is a resting card and which is a modal — so the composites live at tier 2 as --elevation-1…6. A `--shadow-200` at this tier would be an ordinal name for an intent, which is the same misfiling that put --transition-fast in tier 1.

offset-x.$description: Horizontal cast, shared by every step. This is the one axis with a single value rather than a ramp: all six shadows in the system are cast straight down, so a per-step ramp would be six copies of `0`. Same reasoning as --border-width-default — an axis gets a ramp when it HAS one.

offset-y.$description: Vertical cast. Climbs with the step, and faster at the top end — 8px to 20px between 400 and 500 — because 500 is the full-screen overlay tier, not the next notch on a card ramp.

blur.$description: Softness. Always several times the y offset — that ratio is what reads as distance from the surface rather than a hard drop line.

spread.$description: Negative from 200 up, pulling the shadow in so a wide blur does not bleed past the element's own footprint. 050 and 100 are too tight to need it; 500 deliberately does NOT pull in, because a full-screen overlay wants the bleed.

color.$description: The axis that was doing real damage fused. Every shadow ended in a hardcoded rgba(0,0,0,α), so a theme could not tint its shadows at all — split out, six tokens re-point them. Deliberately NOT aliased onto the black-a ramp: black-a starts at 0.05 and steps in units of 0.05, and these alphas are 0.03 / 0.04 / 0.06 / 0.07 / 0.08, so pointing at it would have moved five of the six rendered values. Shadow alpha is its own fine-grained ramp for a reason — the difference between 0.03 and 0.05 is the difference between a card resting and a card lifting.
